project.name: Halden plan-to-produce eval
project.problemStatement: Plan-to-produce at Halden Precision Engineering runs on CAD exports, spreadsheets and a basic job-tracking tool, so engineering changes do not reach the shop floor, material shortages stop projects, project costs are known only after delivery and quality records are paper.

opening: We are Halden Precision Engineering (fictional), a UK maker of custom industrial presses and handling systems with about £95 million revenue, a fabrication works in Sheffield and an assembly and test site in Bristol. Most of our business is engineer-to-order: each machine is a project of 4 to 14 months with its own bill of materials. Engineers design in Aurora PLM and export parts lists to Excel, planners build material requirements by hand, purchasing chases long-lead castings and drives by email, and the shop floor works from printed routings and paper job cards in a basic job-tracking tool. Engineering changes reach the shop late, projects regularly stop for missing parts, and we only learn the true cost of a project after delivery. Quality records are paper, and customers increasingly ask for inspection certificates. Only 71% of machines ship on the promised date. We want to move to SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud within fourteen months.

catalog.process_owner: The Operations Director owns the process from contract to delivery, the Chief Engineer owns bills of materials and engineering changes, and the Finance Controller owns project costing and billing.
catalog.scope_boundary: The process starts when a customer contract is signed and ends when the machine is delivered, billed and the project is closed with a cost variance review. It covers the Sheffield and Bristol sites, engineered-to-order machines and spare assemblies, and excludes aftermarket service contracts.
catalog.current_trigger: A customer contract or purchase order is signed, and the project manager opens a project folder and a spreadsheet budget.
catalog.current_systems: We use Aurora PLM for CAD and engineering bills of materials, Excel for quotes, budgets, material planning and the production schedule, a basic job-tracking tool for shop-floor job cards, paper for inspection records, and a small accounting package for invoicing and ledgers. Parts lists are exported from Aurora PLM and re-keyed.
catalog.current_rules: Engineering changes need the Chief Engineer's sign-off on a paper form. Purchases above £20,000 need the Operations Director's approval. A machine is invoiced in stages agreed in the contract: 30% on order, 40% at factory acceptance and 30% on delivery.
catalog.current_exceptions: Engineering changes after release are passed on to the shop by email and often missed. Parts that fail inspection are scrapped or reworked on a paper non-conformance note. Supplier delays are handled by phone and the schedule is not updated.
catalog.current_financial: Project budgets are Excel files. Costs are collected from supplier invoices and timesheets and compared with the budget only at project close. Work in progress is estimated each quarter. Staged invoices are raised by hand from the contract.
catalog.desired_outcome: On-time delivery of at least 92%, project cost variance under 5% against budget with margin visible during the project, material shortages stopping production reduced by half, and inspection certificates produced from the system.
catalog.desired_controls: We need engineering change control that updates the bill of materials and open production orders, project-based costing with work in progress and settlement, material requirements planning that respects project stock, quality inspection with certificates and non-conformance records, and approval workflow for purchases. Aurora PLM stays as the engineering system and must be integrated, and we prefer standard SAP over custom development.
catalog.process_overview: The process runs in these stages. Estimate and quote the machine: The sales engineer sketches the machine in Aurora PLM, estimates material, labour and test hours in an Excel template and issues a quote with a delivery date based on experience. Create contract and project budget: The project manager copies the estimate into a budget spreadsheet by work package, opens a project folder and agrees the milestone billing plan with finance. Release engineering bill of materials: The engineer completes the design in Aurora PLM, exports the engineering parts list to Excel and sends it to production planning. Build manufacturing bill of materials and routing: The planner turns the parts list into a manufacturing structure in Excel, adds make or buy decisions, and writes routings with operations, work centres and standard hours on printed sheets. Plan material requirements: The planner nets requirements against stock by hand in Excel, ignores stock reserved for other projects and creates a list of items to buy. Buy long-lead and standard parts: The buyer sends enquiries by email, places orders for castings, drives and bought-in parts, and records them in the accounting package. Schedule and run production: The supervisor assigns jobs from the Excel schedule, prints job cards, and operators clock on and off jobs in the job-tracking tool. Inspect and certify: The inspector measures against the drawing, records results on a paper sheet, signs it and prepares a certificate in Word at final inspection and factory acceptance test. Collect project costs and work in progress: The accountant allocates supplier invoices and timesheet hours to project budget spreadsheets by hand and estimates work in progress each quarter. Deliver and bill by milestone: The project manager emails finance when factory acceptance or delivery is reached, finance raises the staged invoice by hand against the contract and logistics books the transport. Close project and review variances: The controller compares final cost with the original budget in Excel and writes a lessons-learned note.
catalog.operating_scale: We have about £95 million revenue and run projects of 4 to 14 months, each with its own bill of materials, from a fabrication works in Sheffield and an assembly and test site in Bristol.
catalog.legal_entities: There is one legal entity, Halden Precision Engineering Ltd, with a fabrication works in Sheffield and an assembly and test site in Bristol.
catalog.target_org_units: We plan one company code 4000 for Halden Precision Engineering, plant 4100 for Sheffield, plant 4200 for Bristol and sales organisation 4000 for Halden Sales UK.
catalog.modules_in_scope: The scope covers production planning, project systems, materials management, quality management, controlling and sales and distribution.
catalog.retained_systems: Aurora PLM stays as the engineering system and must be integrated with SAP. The Excel plans, the job-tracking tool and the small accounting package are replaced.
catalog.external_parties: We deal with customers who ask for inspection certificates, suppliers of long-lead castings, and transport providers for delivery.
catalog.kpi_baselines: Today only 71% of machines ship on the promised date, project cost is known only after delivery, and projects regularly stop for missing parts.
catalog.kpi_targets: On-time delivery of at least 92%, project cost variance under 5% against budget with margin visible during the project, and material shortages stopping production reduced by half.
catalog.timeline: We want to be live on SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud within fourteen months.
catalog.constraints: We prefer standard SAP over custom development. Aurora PLM is kept and integrated, and the job-tracking tool and Excel schedules are retired.
catalog.localization_compliance: Customers increasingly ask for inspection certificates, so quality records must be kept in the system, and UK VAT applies to billing.
catalog.approval_rules: Engineering changes need the Chief Engineer's sign-off on a paper form, and purchases above £20,000 need the Operations Director's approval.
catalog.required_outputs: We need inspection certificates, non-conformance records, a project cost and margin report, the staged contract invoices and a delivery schedule.

steps.name: Estimate and quote the machine
steps.description: The sales engineer sketches the machine in Aurora PLM, estimates material, labour and test hours in an Excel template and issues a quote with a delivery date based on experience.
steps.inputs: Customer specification; previous project costs; supplier quotes
steps.controls: The Operations Director approves quotes above £250,000
steps.exceptions: When the specification changes the estimate is rebuilt and the quoted margin is rarely revisited.

steps.name: Create contract and project budget
steps.description: The project manager copies the estimate into a budget spreadsheet by work package, opens a project folder and agrees the milestone billing plan with finance. There is no project number in any system.
steps.inputs: Signed contract; estimate; milestone billing plan
steps.controls: The Finance Controller reviews the budget for projects above £500,000
steps.exceptions: Scope changes agreed with the customer are added to the budget by hand and sometimes not billed.

steps.name: Release engineering bill of materials
steps.trigger: The design is approved by the Chief Engineer.
steps.description: The engineer completes the design in Aurora PLM, exports the engineering parts list to Excel and sends it to production planning. Revisions are tracked inside Aurora PLM only.
steps.inputs: Approved design; part library; revision history
steps.controls: The Chief Engineer signs off the release on a paper form
steps.exceptions: A change after release is emailed to planning and the old parts list stays in use until someone notices.

steps.name: Build manufacturing bill of materials and routing
steps.trigger: The engineering parts list is received.
steps.description: The planner turns the parts list into a manufacturing structure in Excel, adds make or buy decisions, and writes routings with operations, work centres and standard hours on printed sheets.
steps.inputs: Engineering parts list; routing templates; work centre list
steps.controls: The production manager reviews routings for large projects
steps.exceptions: Parts missing from the export are found when the shop asks for them.

steps.name: Plan material requirements
steps.description: The planner nets requirements against stock by hand in Excel, ignores stock reserved for other projects and creates a list of items to buy. Lead times come from a supplier sheet that is rarely updated.
steps.inputs: Manufacturing structure; stock list; supplier lead time sheet
steps.controls: None, it depends on the planner's judgement
steps.exceptions: Stock meant for one project is used for another, so the first project later stops for missing parts.

steps.name: Buy long-lead and standard parts
steps.description: The buyer sends enquiries by email, places orders for castings, drives and bought-in parts, and records them in the accounting package. Order delivery dates are kept in the buyer's own spreadsheet.
steps.inputs: Purchase list; supplier quotes; project budget
steps.controls: The Operations Director approves purchases above £20,000
steps.exceptions: Late deliveries are chased by phone and the production schedule is not updated.

steps.name: Schedule and run production
steps.system: Job-tracking tool, printed job cards and Excel schedule
steps.trigger: Material is available and the schedule slot is reached.
steps.description: The supervisor assigns jobs from the Excel schedule, prints job cards, and operators clock on and off jobs in the job-tracking tool. Capacity per work centre is checked by experience.
steps.inputs: Excel schedule; job cards; material issued from stores
steps.outputs: Fabricated parts and sub-assemblies; job card hours
steps.controls: The supervisor checks material against the printed parts list
steps.exceptions: Urgent jobs are slotted in without updating the schedule, and missing parts are discovered at assembly.

steps.name: Inspect and certify
steps.trigger: A fabricated part or the assembled machine is ready for inspection.
steps.description: The inspector measures against the drawing, records results on a paper sheet, signs it and prepares a certificate in Word at final inspection and factory acceptance test.
steps.controls: Final inspection is signed by the quality manager
steps.exceptions: A failed part is reworked or scrapped on a paper non-conformance note that is not linked to the project cost.

steps.name: Collect project costs and work in progress
steps.description: The accountant allocates supplier invoices and timesheet hours to project budget spreadsheets by hand and estimates work in progress each quarter. Actual margin is known only after delivery.
steps.inputs: Supplier invoices; timesheet hours; project budget spreadsheet
steps.outputs: Project cost report in Excel; quarterly WIP estimate
steps.controls: The Finance Controller reviews the project cost report
steps.exceptions: Costs booked to the wrong project are found at project close.

steps.name: Deliver and bill by milestone
steps.description: The project manager emails finance when factory acceptance or delivery is reached, finance raises the staged invoice by hand against the contract and logistics books the transport. Customer sign-off is a paper form.
steps.inputs: Contract billing plan; acceptance certificate; delivery note
steps.outputs: Staged invoice; delivery note; signed acceptance form
steps.controls: The Finance Controller approves invoices above £100,000
steps.exceptions: Invoices are delayed when the acceptance form arrives late, and scope extras are not billed.

steps.name: Close project and review variances
steps.trigger: The final invoice is paid and warranty starts.
steps.description: The controller compares final cost with the original budget in Excel and writes a lessons-learned note. Estimating templates are rarely updated from actual results.
steps.inputs: Final project cost report; budget spreadsheet; non-conformance notes
steps.controls: The Operations Director reviews the variance note
steps.exceptions: Warranty costs after delivery are not linked to the project.

requirements.statement: Aurora PLM stays as the engineering design system and must be integrated with SAP for the bill of materials and changes, not replaced.
Engineering changes after release are emailed to planning and the old parts list stays in use, so the shop builds to outdated revisions.
The manufacturing bill of materials and routings are built by hand in Excel and on printed sheets, and parts are missing from the export.
Material requirements are netted by hand and stock reserved for one project is used for another, so projects stop for missing parts.
Material shortages that stop production must be cut by half through automatic requirements planning per project.
Supplier delivery dates sit in the buyer's own spreadsheet and the production schedule is not updated when castings or drives are late.
Purchases above £20,000 must be approved by the Operations Director in the system.
Capacity per work centre is checked by experience, and urgent jobs are slotted in without updating the schedule.
Inspection results and non-conformances are on paper and certificates are written in Word, with no link to the project cost.
Project costs are allocated by hand and margin is known only after delivery, with work in progress estimated quarterly.
Project cost variance must stay under 5% against budget with margin visible during the project.
Staged invoices are raised by hand from the contract, so milestones are billed late and scope extras are missed.
On-time delivery must reach at least 92%, up from 71%.
